persona.name: Sanjay Gupta
persona.background: He works long hours outdoors in a hot, humid environment and often sweats heavily while wearing tight work clothing. He has noticed recurrent skin color changes over his upper body that become more obvious after sun exposure.

diagnoses.name: Pityriasis versicolor (Tinea versicolor)
diagnoses.description: A relatively common persistent superficial skin condition caused by the commensal lipophilic yeast Malassezia furfur; typical lesions are round/oval scaly macules on the upper trunk, often hypopigmented and more obvious after sun exposure.

diagnoses.name: Vitiligo
diagnoses.description: A common, slowly progressive acquired condition caused by focal loss of melanocytes resulting in well-circumscribed depigmented patches, often symmetrical and occurring around body orifices, hands, feet, flexor wrists, ankles, elbows, knees, and major body folds.

diagnoses.name: Pityriasis alba
diagnoses.description: A common skin disorder in children usually evident before puberty, presenting with hypopigmented patches or macules with slight scale mainly on the face and less frequently on the neck, trunk, and extremities.

diagnoses.name: Atopic dermatitis (Atopic eczema)
diagnoses.description: An endogenous eczema in atopic individuals; extremely itchy erythematous scaly patches with scratching, xeroderma, and in chronic cases lichenification, with distribution often in periorbital and flexor areas.

diagnoses.name: Seborrheic dermatitis
diagnoses.description: An erythematous scaling disorder affecting nasolabial folds, eyebrows, eyelids, glabella, scalp (dandruff), and sometimes chest/axilla/groin; in young adults (especially males) it tends to be persistent.

diagnoses.name: Plaque psoriasis (Psoriasis vulgaris)
diagnoses.description: The most common form of psoriasis with symmetrically distributed well-defined plaques (1–10 cm) with raised margins and thick silvery scales, commonly involving scalp and extensor surfaces; Koebner phenomenon may occur.

diagnoses.name: Lichen planus
diagnoses.description: Pruritic planar purple polygonal papules/plaques (the '5 P's') often on flexor wrists, flanks, medial thighs, shins, glans penis, nails, scalp, and oral mucosa; Wickham’s striae and Koebner’s phenomenon may be present.

diagnoses.name: Erythema multiforme
diagnoses.description: An acute, self-limiting, recurrent cutaneous and/or mucocutaneous blistering eruption characterized by target-shaped plaques commonly over extremities and face; lesions are symmetrical, acral, and centripetal.

diagnoses.name: Stevens–Johnson syndrome (SJS)
diagnoses.description: A rare, acute, life-threatening mucocutaneous disease with systemic involvement, nearly always drug-related, with <10% body surface area detachment and mucosal involvement at least two sites.

diagnoses.name: Bullous pemphigoid
diagnoses.description: A chronic relapsing blistering disorder in the elderly characterized by itchy, tense bullae with usually negative Nikolsky sign and mucosal involvement in 10–30%.

symptoms:

precomputedExplanations.description: **Pityriasis versicolor (Tinea versicolor)** is a superficial fungal infection caused by Malassezia species affecting the stratum corneum. It produces hypo- or hyperpigmented, finely scaly macules on the upper trunk that often become more noticeable after sun exposure due to impaired tanning.
keySymptoms: **Hypopigmented macules** - Reduced pigmentation becomes prominent after tanning because affected skin fails to tan normally.
**Fine scale** - Subtle branny scaling supports superficial stratum corneum involvement typical of Malassezia overgrowth.
**Upper trunk distribution** - Predilection for chest, back, and shoulders aligns with sebum-rich Malassezia colonization sites.
**Round/oval scaly patches** - Classic morphology of pityriasis versicolor lesions helps distinguish from vitiligo or pityriasis alba.
**Persistence for months** - Chronic, recurrent course is common, especially in warm climates or with sweating/oily skin.
**More noticeable after sun exposure** - Contrast increases as surrounding skin tans while involved areas remain lighter.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: The patient has chronic, round/oval, finely scaly hypopigmented macules on the upper back and chest that become more apparent after sun exposure, which is characteristic of **pityriasis versicolor**. The distribution on the upper trunk and shoulders strongly fits Malassezia-related disease in sebum-rich areas. The fine scale supports a superficial fungal process rather than depigmenting disorders like **vitiligo** (typically no scale). Confirmatory bedside tests would include KOH scraping showing **"spaghetti and meatballs"** hyphae/yeast and **Wood’s lamp** yellow fluorescence.

precomputedExplanations.description: **Vitiligo** is an acquired disorder of pigmentation caused by autoimmune destruction of melanocytes, producing well-demarcated depigmented patches. Lesions are typically non-scaly and may be associated with other autoimmune diseases.
keySymptoms: **Depigmented macules/patches** - Chalk-white, complete pigment loss with sharp borders, often enlarging over time.
**No surface scale** - Lesions feel smooth without fine branny scaling on rubbing or scraping.
**Periorificial/acral distribution** - Common on face, hands, feet, and around mouth, eyes, genitals.
**Koebner phenomenon** - New lesions can appear at sites of trauma, friction, or pressure.
**Leukotrichia** - Whitening of hair within lesions suggests melanocyte loss in follicles.
**Autoimmune association** - Increased risk with thyroid disease, type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, alopecia areata.
precomputedExplanations.clinicalReasoning: This patient has hypopigmented round/oval macules on the upper trunk with **fine scale** and increased visibility after sun exposure. That pattern strongly suggests **Malassezia**-related **pityriasis versicolor**, which commonly affects the back, shoulders, and chest and produces branny scaling. In contrast, **vitiligo** causes smooth, non-scaly, sharply demarcated depigmented patches and typically has a different distribution. The persistence with scale and classic trunk distribution makes vitiligo unlikely.
precomputedExplanations.whyIncorrectForCase: The lesions described are **scaly** and located on the **upper trunk**, which is typical for **pityriasis versicolor** but not for **vitiligo**. Vitiligo usually presents as **chalk-white depigmentation without scale**, often involving face and acral/periorificial sites.

**Distribution** - Vitiligo favors face, hands, periorificial areas; **pityriasis versicolor** favors upper back, shoulders, chest.
